title: In 1854 a doctor traced a deadly cholera outbreak to one water pump

cover.alt: A cast-iron street pump at dusk on a London street of brick houses, with a man in a black frock coat holding a sheet of paper beside it.

body: In ten days in 1854, cholera killed more than 500 people within a few streets of Broad Street in Soho, London. Most doctors blamed miasma, a poison in foul air, but **John Snow** tracked the deaths to the water of one street pump, and on his evidence the parish took off its handle on 8 September, though the outbreak was already falling away. The General Board of Health rejected his explanation. Then the curate **Henry Whitehead**, who had expected to disprove Snow, traced the probable first case to a house whose cesspool lay beside the well. Snow’s map of the deaths, drawn that December, became a classic of epidemiology.

slides.alt: A busy street of brick terraces. A woman works the long handle of a cast-iron street pump while water runs into a pail; a girl waits with a jug, a woman in a bonnet brings another, and a man carries two full pails away.
slides.caption: Soho, London, the summer of 1854. Families on Broad Street draw their drinking water from the street pump.

slides.alt: Night. A handcart carries two coffins down the street. In a doorway hung with black crepe a woman in a white cap looks out, frightened, at a grey-whiskered doctor in a top hat who holds a handkerchief to his face.
slides.caption: From the night of 31 August, cholera tears through the streets. In ten days, over 500 people die within 250 yards.

bubbles.text: It is miasma, madam: a poison in the foul air.
bubbles.speaker: A doctor

slides.alt: John Snow, a clean-shaven man in a black frock coat, stands in the foreground holding a list. Behind him is the pump, a half-empty street and doors hung with black crepe.
slides.caption: Dr John Snow has argued since 1849 that cholera spreads through dirty water. He takes a list of the dead and goes to the spot.

bubbles.text: Nearly all the deaths are within a short distance of the pump.
bubbles.speaker: John Snow

slides.alt: Inside a brick brewery with a great vat and barrels, Snow talks to Mr Huggins, an older man with grey side-whiskers in a brown coat. Behind them two workmen in aprons drink from tankards.
slides.caption: Near the pump is a brewery with above seventy workmen. None is on the list of the dead, so Snow calls on its owner.

bubbles.text: Have your men suffered from the cholera?
bubbles.speaker: John Snow

bubbles.text: None has had it badly, sir. They have their malt liquor and never take water from the pump.
bubbles.speaker: Mr Huggins

slides.alt: In a parlour with green wallpaper, an elderly widow in black and a white cap pours water from a large green bottle into a glass. Through the window are green hills and trees.
slides.caption: In Hampstead, where there is no cholera, a widow has a bottle of Broad Street water brought by cart every day. She prefers it.

bubbles.text: She drank it on the Thursday and the Friday. She died on the Saturday.
bubbles.speaker: Her son

slides.alt: A panelled room lit by gas. Four stern gentlemen sit behind a table covered in green baize and papers. Snow stands at the end of the table with his papers, his other hand held out to them.
slides.caption: Thursday 7 September, evening. Snow puts the facts to the Board of Guardians of St James’s parish.

bubbles.text: There is no outbreak here except among those who drink from that pump-well.
bubbles.speaker: John Snow

slides.alt: Daylight on Broad Street. A workman in an apron and cap holds the pump handle he has just taken off; the pump stands without it. A parish officer in a top hat holds an order, and three neighbours watch.
slides.caption: Friday 8 September: the handle comes off. But new fatal cases had already fallen, from 143 on 1 September to 12.

bubbles.text: Where will we get our water now?
bubbles.speaker: A boy

slides.alt: A cutaway below the street. Under the front area of No. 40 lies a brick cesspool of foul water; its drain leaks through the soil into the brick shaft of the pump’s well beside it. The curate Henry Whitehead stands on the pavement above, pointing down.
slides.caption: Months later, the curate Henry Whitehead traced the probable first case.

bubbles.text: A baby at No. 40 fell ill on 28 August. Some of the water from her nappies went into this cesspool.
bubbles.speaker: Henry Whitehead

slides.question: Why did the brewery’s workmen escape the cholera?
options: They drank beer, not pump water
slides.explanation: The men had an allowance of malt liquor and never drank from the pump. Their luck pointed to the water, not the air.

source.label: John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (1855)
